Ideally, upon reading your abstract, the reader should feel he / she must read your paper in entirety.

# Introduction \label{Introduction}



The goal is to comment on two statements:

The South African rand (ZAR) has been one of the most volatile currencies.

The ZAR performs well during favorable G10 carry trade conditions and when the USD is strong (risk-on).

We are to measure volatility, compare currencies, and use tables, graphs, stratification, and statistics.





Steps:

Load the necessary data and packages.

Calculate returns and clean the data (if not already done).

Measure volatility: we can use standard deviation, but also GARCH models to capture time-varying volatility.

Compare the volatility of ZAR to other currencies.

Analyze the relationship between ZAR and carry trade conditions (using the carry data) and the strength of the USD (using BBDXY).

We are to use univariate GARCH for volatility and multivariate GARCH (DCC, GO-GARCH) for correlation

We will:

Load the data and calculate log returns for the currencies.

Use univariate GARCH to model the volatility of ZAR and other currencies, and compare.

Use multivariate GARCH (DCC and GO-GARCH) to study the time-varying correlation between ZAR and other currencies, and between ZAR and the dollar index (BBDXY) and carry trade conditions.

Volatility Persistence: Show if ZAR has higher GARCH persistence (α + β) than peers

Leverage Effects: Use gjrGARCH or eGARCH to test if negative shocks have larger impact

Regime Dependence: Demonstrate how ZAR volatility and correlations change with:

Dollar strength periods

Carry trade favorable environments

Risk-on/risk-off episodes (using VIX)

Forecast Performance: Use rolling GARCH to show VaR accuracy for ZAR


```{R}
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and tidy currency returns (all vs USD)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  lubridate,
  tbl2xts,
  PerformanceAnalytics,
  ggthemes,
  RcppRoll
)

cncy   <- readr::read_rds("data/currencies.rds")      # wide: date + currencies
Carry  <- readr::read_rds("data/cncyCarry.rds")       # global carry factor / panel
value  <- readr::read_rds("data/cncyvalue.rds")       # currency value factor
cncyIV <- readr::read_rds("data/cncyIV.rds")          # FX implied vols
bbdxy  <- readr::read_rds("data/bbdxy.rds")           # Bloomberg Dollar Index

# Assume cncy is wide: date + one column per currency return (e.g. "ZAR", "EUR", "GBP", ...)
cncy_long <- 
  cncy %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "ccy",
    values_to = "ret"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    year = year(date)
  )

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Annualised realised volatility by year and currency
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
vol_annual <- 
  cncy_long %>% 
  group_by(ccy, year) %>% 
  summarise(
    ann_sd  = sd(ret, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252),
    ann_var = var(ret, na.rm = TRUE) * 252,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Rank currencies by typical volatility over the sample
vol_rank <- 
  vol_annual %>% 
  group_by(ccy) %>% 
  summarise(
    mean_ann_sd = mean(ann_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75_ann_sd  = quantile(ann_sd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean_ann_sd)) %>% 
  mutate(rank = row_number())

# Nice table with ZAR highlighted
vol_rank %>% 
  mutate(
    is_ZAR = if_else(ccy == "ZAR", "ZAR", "Other")
  ) %>% 
  arrange(rank)

```
